evidence_quotes.quote: It results from an action-research project that adopted a price-based methodology, and involved a researcher, the author, and high level sector stakeholders, in a one-year participatory process, for defining a water policy that would be equitable for users and financially sustainable for private operators engaged in ten-year affermage contracts.

develop a financial modelling and design a tariff policy that could meet political expectations. The scope of the modelling and policy covers 2,047 small towns ranging from 2,000 to 10,000 inhabitants (Pezon, 2015b).

The researcher proposed a tariff-based approach where the tariff does not stand as the outcome of the research but its starting point. Subsequently, the research question becomes: under which conditions the targeted tariff is compatible with the financial sustainability of the service? The methodology then consisted of developing a financial modelling that gives, for a set tariff, the profit margin of the operators over ten-year contracts, based on variables such as demand (demographic growth, consumption, type of service, and density), investment (production and distribution of water) and operating cost.

Is it financially sustainable for operators to provide access to water to 11.8 million people at half price? Under what conditions can the targeted tariffs cover the operation, maintenance and capital maintenance expenditure for pumps and generators, and spare a decent profit to the private sector?
The water tariff policy has been presented to the new ministry of water and incorporated in the 2016–2030 WASH strategy in view of submission to the council of ministers.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines strategies for achieving universal household and community drinking-water access (stand-pipe basic service and on-plot piped private connections) in 2,047 small towns (2,000 to 10,000 inhabitants) in Burkina Faso.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it examines regulatory, contractual, and tariff governance of semi-urban water supply. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly addresses rule-type mechanisms—tariff and cost-recovery rules (volumetric tariffs, monthly fixed fees, free versus charged private connection fees, and capital-maintenance renewal provisions) and utility regulatory/contractual structure (price-cap regulation of private operators under ten-year affermage contracts)—although in the quantitative simulations (Sections 4-5) the proposed tariff rules are held fixed as starting assumptions while pumping energy source (solar versus fossil fuel) is varied.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evaluation of service access. The paper reports a participatory policy-design ('action-research') process with sector working groups to set normative 2016-2030 tariff and coverage targets and engineering unit-cost assumptions (Annex 2), coupled with a prospective ex-ante deterministic financial simulation model for 2016-2030. The proposed tariff and price-cap policy had not yet been enacted (it was awaiting submission to the Council of Ministers), and brief mentions of existing scheme functionality (67%) or consumption (10-15 l/c/d) merely cite secondary reports (e.g., Pezon, 2013) as background context.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report an empirically measured household or community access outcome. In the financial simulation model, phased service coverage (35% to 100%, Table 2), daily per-capita consumption (8 to 20 l/c/d, Table 3), and halved tariffs with free connections (250/500 FCFA/m3) are entered as exogenous policy targets and forecast assumptions, whereas the simulated outputs are private operator unit O&M costs, 10-year/15-year operating profits and profit margins, and required public capital investment (CAPEX).
criterion_notes.c5: While the target population (2,047 small towns in Burkina Faso) and prospective simulation structure are clearly described, there is no empirically observed exposure-to-access-outcome design evaluating how a legal or regulatory mechanism affects realized household or community water access.

study_design: Participatory action-research policy design and prospective ex-ante financial simulation modelling (2016-2030)
population_and_sample: 2,047 small towns (2,000 to 10,000 inhabitants; projected 11.8 million residents by 2030) in Burkina Faso modeled in prospective 2016-2030 simulations, parameterized by four stakeholder working groups, two national workshops (80 participants), and an annual sector forum (250 participants)
exposure: Proposed price-cap tariff policy (250 FCFA/m3 at stand-pipes, 500 FCFA/m3 and 500 FCFA/month on-plot with free private connections) under 10-year private affermage contracts, comparing solar energy versus fossil-fuel groundwater pumping in prospective financial simulations
outcome: Simulated unit operation and maintenance expenditure (FCFA/m3), 10-year and 15-year private operator operating profits and profit margins (%), and required capital investment (CAPEX); water access coverage and per-capita consumption are assumed exogenous model inputs rather than empirically measured outcomes
rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper addresses drinking-water access in small towns in Burkina Faso (c1=yes) and discusses rule-type regulatory and tariff mechanisms including price-cap regulation, volumetric/connection tariff rules, and 10-year private affermage contracts (c2=yes under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 reading), it is a prospective policy-design ('action-research') and ex-ante deterministic financial simulation study for 2016-2030 rather than an empirical evaluation of water service access (c3=no). Stakeholder working groups agreed on normative target tariffs, phased 2016-2030 universal coverage targets (Table 2), demand forecasts (Table 3), and standard engineering unit-cost assumptions (Annex 2) to simulate operator operating profit margins and required public CAPEX under solar versus fossil-fuel pumping, and the proposed policy had not yet been enacted. Moreover, household access coverage, consumption, and target tariffs are exogenous model assumptions rather than empirically measured access outcomes (c4=no).
